title: Connect your own workflow stage
description: Learn the worker contract: register an operation, consume a run and return one durable result.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Imagine a fictional integrator with a service that processes recordings. When is a custom stage the right fit?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use a stage when you control the deployment and want the workflow engine to trigger processing automatically. If your producer simply has data to push, the ingest API may be a simpler starting point. Workers outside the deployment have a separate external-stage boundary.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So a custom stage isn't a requirement for every integration?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Correct. Pick the trigger and trust boundary first. Don't give an external worker the internal run contract just because both paths eventually return useful results.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What connects our worker to the definition?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The operation identifies the stage, its routing result and its completion. Register the stage in the workflow and deploy the matching worker with the correct queue. Routing without a consumer doesn't create a working service.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can the stage wait for an earlier result to meet a condition?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Yes, conditional routing checks the configured needs against available context and results. Use the documented field paths and operators, then inspect routing decisions with a real run rather than assuming a condition means what its label suggests.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: The worker finishes. Does it have to maintain its own Hub database writes?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Usually not. It can return supported typed blocks for Hub to validate and persist. A worker owning genuinely separate storage instead returns its routing values. Use exactly one result channel, retain the run's identity and context, and clear storage credentials on the return message.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And completing the computation isn't enough?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The worker must hand the completed result back to the engine. Make writes idempotent because delivery can repeat. Follow one recording through dispatch, persistence and resolution before scaling out. The built-in analysis continues independently, so an ordinary recording appearing in Hub does not prove your stage completed.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.
